imgs.a: Two karyotypes, A showing trisomy 21 and B showing an extra sex chromosome

qs.q: What percentage of Down syndrome cases are caused by trisomy 21?
qs.e: About 95% of affected persons with Down syndrome have trisomy 21, with a chromosome count of 47, most commonly caused by meiotic nondisjunction.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What is the maternal age-related incidence of Down syndrome in women older than 45 years?
o: Limited to a single tissue compartment
qs.e: Down syndrome occurs in 1 in 1550 live births in women younger than 20 years but increases dramatically to 1 in 25 live births in women older than 45 years.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: In what percentage of Down syndrome cases is the extra chromosome of maternal origin?
qs.e: In 95% of Down syndrome cases, the extra chromosome is of maternal origin, supporting that meiotic nondisjunction occurs primarily in the ovum.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What percentage of Down syndrome cases result from translocation?
qs.e: In about 4% of all patients with trisomy 21, the extra chromosomal material is present as a translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to chromosome 22 or 14.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What percentage of Down syndrome patients are mosaics?
qs.e: Approximately 1% of patients with trisomy 21 are mosaics, usually having a mixture of 46- and 47-chromosome cells resulting from mitotic nondisjunction during embryogenesis.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What percentage of Down syndrome patients have congenital heart disease?
qs.e: Approximately 40% of Down syndrome patients have congenital heart disease, most commonly endocardial cushion defects including atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What is the increased risk of acute leukemia in children with Down syndrome?
qs.e: Children with trisomy 21 have a 10- to 20-fold increased risk of developing acute leukemia, including both acute lymphoblastic leukemias and acute myeloid leukemias.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

qs.q: What is the current median age at death for persons with Down syndrome?
qs.e: Improved medical care has increased the longevity of persons with trisomy 21, with the current median age at death being 47 years, up from 25 years in 1983.
qs.s: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs

ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by trisomy 21, leading to characteristic facial features, developmental delay, and multiple organ system involvement, especially congenital heart disease.

sections.p: Down syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, most often from nondisjunction. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype showing 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21.
b: Clinical suspicion: flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease.
Prenatal screening: nuchal translucency, serum PAPP‑A, free β‑hCG.
Post‑natal confirmatory test: chromosomal analysis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by functional domains (cognitive, cardiac, endocrine) rather than a single stage. The American Academy of Pediatrics uses risk‑based categories for cardiac lesions and developmental milestones.
b: Mild: normal IQ >70, no major organ defects.
Moderate: IQ 50‑70, treatable cardiac lesion.
Severe: IQ <50, multiple organ involvement.

sections.p: The overwhelming cause is meiotic nondisjunction (≈95%). Translocation (≈4%) and mosaicism (<1%) are less common.
b: Maternal age >35 years increases nondisjunction risk.
Paternal translocation can be inherited in families.

sections.p: Newborns show hypotonia, up‑slanting palpebral fissures, single transverse palmar crease, and a protruding tongue. Developmental delay becomes evident by 6‑12 months.
b: Congenital heart disease in 40‑50% (AV septal defect most common).
Increased risk of duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, and early‑onset Alzheimer’s.

sections.p: Investigations focus on confirming the genetic diagnosis and identifying associated organ anomalies.

t.b: Confirms trisomy 21; a result of 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 establishes diagnosis.
Detects structural heart disease; identifies AV septal defect, VSD, or PDA guiding surgical timing.
Screens for congenital hypothyroidism; elevated TSH indicates need for replacement.
Detects conductive or sensorineural loss; abnormal result prompts audiology referral.
Clinical exam for murmurs + chest X‑ray can suggest cardiac shunts; refer urgently for cardiac evaluation.

sections.p: Complications often arise from cardiac, respiratory, or endocrine problems and can be life‑threatening.
b: Severe cyanotic heart disease causing failure to thrive.
Obstructive sleep apnea leading to hypoxia.
Acute leukemia (especially ALL) presenting with pallor, bruising.

sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: correct cardiac lesions, monitor endocrine function, support development, and prevent infections.
b: Surgical repair of AV septal defect or VSD when indicated.
Levothyroxine for hypothyroidism; chosen for safety and ease of monitoring.
Early intervention services (physiotherapy, speech, occupational therapy).
Vaccinations per schedule; extra vigilance for respiratory infections.

sections.p: Regular follow‑up tracks growth, cardiac status, thyroid function, and developmental progress.
b: Cardiology review every 6‑12 months until repair, then annually.
Thyroid tests at birth, 6 months, then yearly.
Vision and hearing screening at least annually.

sections.p: Conditions sharing facial features or developmental delay can be mistaken for Down syndrome.
b: Williams syndrome (elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis).
Noonan syndrome (short stature, cardiac defects).
Mosaic trisomy 8 (similar dysmorphic features).

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite underlying pathology.
b: Normal newborn hearing screen can miss later‑onset conductive loss from otitis media.
Mildly elevated TSH may be ignored; early treatment prevents neurocognitive decline.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden cyanosis or worsening murmur indicating cardiac decompensation.
High fever with lethargy suggesting sepsis or meningitis.
Rapid weight loss or feeding difficulty causing dehydration.

faq.q: Why is AV septal defect the most common heart lesion in Down syndrome?
faq.a: Trisomy 21 disrupts endocardial cushion development, leading to AV canal defects.
No, but pre‑conception counseling and prenatal screening can identify risk.

faq.q: Do all children with Down syndrome need surgery?
faq.a: Only those with clinically significant cardiac or gastrointestinal anomalies require operative intervention.

exam: Describe the genetic mechanisms leading to Down syndrome and the most common cardiac anomaly.
List the key screening investigations for a newborn with suspected Down syndrome and interpret their results.
